title: Lesson Observation is Easy
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Dominic Salles, a former senior leader with 26 years in schools, proposes a simple scoring checklist to help observers decide what feedback to give after watching a lesson. The checklist asks whether a change will make students work harder (5 points), improve the curriculum students remember and do (4 points) and improve how hard they think (3 points), for a maximum of 12. He then applies it to a real observation dialogue in which an observer coaches a maths teacher at length on a purple-pen marking routine. Salles argues that the advice, though sensible, scores only 4 points and misses the larger issue: students sit in groups, which makes it hard for the teacher to see who is still writing and harder to get everyone working hard every lesson. That higher-scoring problem is a 12-point issue, and moving to rows would have far more impact. Even within the routine itself, he says the right fix is "the shortest path": a three-second countdown with students standing so that compliance is instantly visible.
points: A three-question points checklist (5, 4 and 3 points) gives observers a way to rank possible feedback by its likely effect on learning rather than by how good the advice sounds.
Feedback that is correct and well delivered can still be low value if it targets a routine instead of the structural cause of the problem.
Seating students in groups made it harder for the teacher to see who was still writing and lowered how hard students worked in every lesson, making it a 12-point issue.
The "shortest path" test asks for the simplest instruction that makes compliance visible, such as a short countdown and having students stand.
Long, multi-step coaching conversations can bury the one change that would matter most, so observers should choose a single focus.
quotes: Will it make students work hard so they learn as much as possible? (5 points)
Ok, the 3 point checklist helps you decide what to focus on after you have watched the lesson.

For comparison, my school experience lasted 26 years, 8 as a senior leader in charge of teaching and learning and latterly curriculum. This doesn’t make me smarter. It simply means I notice very different things.
This feels like very good advice, doesn’t it. But the checklist says no. It helps you give even better advice.
The countdown is too long. 10! Never use a countdown longer than 5. 3 is actually plenty.
It will be very, very easy to see if a student has refused to stand. Everyone who is standing will not be writing.
What could happen if the teacher used rows instead of groups? Much more impact than any routine around purple pens.
The observation focus should have been: The teacher needs to move away from tables in groups.
